new_platform_errors: Claims Cloudflare documents 100,000 PBKDF2 iterations as the 'practical max' for crypto.subtle — no such specific documented limit exists; Workers CPU-time limits vary by plan and PBKDF2 iteration guidance is not pinned to that number.

Cites a specific version gate '@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers ≥0.16.20' for evictDurableObject/evictAllDurableObjects — this precise version number is asserted without a verifiable source and is likely fabricated specificity.

Claims '@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers (≥0.16.20)' exports 'evictDurableObject'/'evictAllDurableObjects' from 'cloudflare:test', citing a specific '2026-06-25' Cloudflare changelog entry — this exact package version, function names, and changelog date are asserted with unverified precision and are not confirmed accurate.

Claims Cloudflare's `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` package exports `evictDurableObject`/`evictAllDurableObjects` from `cloudflare:test`, citing a specific version floor (0.16.20+) and changelog date (2026-06-25) — this specific API name/version/date is not a verifiable real feature and appears fabricated.

Claims Miniflare 'historically never evicted DOs from memory even when hibernatable WebSocket events fired' — an unverified, overly specific historical claim about Miniflare's internal eviction behavior.
Review claims CacheService.getScriptCache() has a 'global 1,000-item cap' — this is not a documented Apps Script CacheService quota; no such fixed item-count limit exists in the official docs.

The review claims CacheService has 'a soft 1,000-item cap shared across all callers of getScriptCache()' — this is not a documented Google Apps Script CacheService limit; Google's documented constraints are per-key value size (100KB) and per-put expiration (max 21600s/6h), not a fixed item-count cap.

Claims the Apex FOR UPDATE lock-contention failure throws a DmlException after a 10-second timeout — the documented failure mode is a QueryException with message 'UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW', not a DmlException.

Claims 'ORDER BY can't be combined with' FOR UPDATE — Salesforce's documented FOR UPDATE restrictions cover things like aggregate functions/GROUP BY/counting queries, not ORDER BY; this restriction is not a real, documented limitation.

Finding 5's correction says to concatenate Game+row+col+shooter into a 'formula/text field and mark that field Unique' — but Salesforce does not allow the Unique attribute on formula fields (only on stored field types like Text, Number, Email); a formula field's value isn't stored, so it can't be flagged Unique. The concatenated key must live in a regular stored field (e.g., populated via trigger/flow) for Unique to apply, which the review's own correction elides by lumping 'formula/text' together.

Review's fix for Finding 3 assigns Item 1 as 'a field-level security check via Schema.sObjectField.isAccessible()/FLS-enforced SOQL' to confirm that a specific opponent's fleet records/fields are inaccessible to a specific test user — but FLS is a profile/permission-set-wide restriction on a field across all records of an object, not a per-record/per-owner control, so FLS cannot be the mechanism that denies one player visibility into a specific opponent's records while allowing visibility into others; that separation can only come from sharing/ownership rules, which the review misattributes as the Item 9 (not Item 1) concern.

gas_card_1.trust.how: Plan notes apiExec/srv is 'not a trust boundary' and adds named srv.ttt.* wrapper functions, but never restricts apiExec itself — arbitrary new Function() execution remains reachable directly, so any client can still bypass the wrapper and read/write PropertiesService state (hidden fleets) directly.

gas_card_2.trust.how: Plan names apiExec/new Function as a known open trust gap (any signed-in caller can bypass game-server and hit apiExec directly), but takes no action to close it—just documents it as an accepted risk in README.

gas_card_3.trust.how: Plan notes apiExec lets clients invoke any server function directly, and adds seat/turn checks inside game-store.gs's play()/getState(), but doesn't close the underlying new Function exec hole itself — a caller can still bypass those checks by directly invoking PropertiesService/game internals through the same apiExec bridge to read hidden fleet state.

gas_control_1.trust.how: Plan relies on USER_ACCESSING identity and per-game role checks in game-store.gs, but never addresses that the srv/apiExec RPC bridge executes arbitrary client-supplied code via new Function, which would let any authenticated user bypass role checks and read/write any game's PropertiesService state directly.

gas_control_2.trust.how: Plan treats Session.getActiveUser() identity as sufficient and adds turn/membership checks inside game-state.gs, but never addresses that apiExec's new Function() lets any signed-in user call require() directly (bypassing srv.gameState and its checks) or call getState(gid) for any guessable gameId with no membership check, exposing hidden per-player state; no sandboxing/allowlisting of apiExec or per-viewer state filtering is proposed.

gas_control_3.trust.how: Plan adds participant checks (resolveMark/joinRecord) only inside the intended game-store.gs RPC functions, but never addresses that apiExec's `new Function` execution lets any authenticated caller invoke arbitrary code (e.g. call PropertiesService.getScriptProperties().getProperty('TTT_GAME_<id>') directly) bypassing those checks entirely; it also targets tic-tac-toe with a fully public board, so hidden-fleet secrecy was never in scope or discussed.

gas_current_1.trust.how: Plan never mentions apiExec/new Function or that srv.gameStore RPCs let any client send arbitrary code as themselves; it only adds server-side turn/identity checks to the game logic, leaving the eval-based RPC proxy itself unaddressed.

gas_current_2.trust.how: Plan only guards against identity spoofing (never trust client-supplied seat/email, use Session.getActiveUser in play/join). It never treats apiExec's new Function(...) eval as a trust boundary problem: since any signed-in caller can execute arbitrary server code, they can bypass getState()'s redaction and the game-session wrapper entirely to read raw ConfigManager/PropertiesService state (e.g. hidden fleet placement) directly. No mitigation (e.g. splitting eval-exposed dev/MCP functions from a locked-down production API, or storing hidden data where the requesting identity can't reach it via arbitrary eval) is proposed.

gas_current_3.trust.how: Plan focuses on adding identity/turn/lock logic in a new module but never addresses that apiExec executes arbitrary client-submitted code via new Function, letting any user bypass ttt-match's validation entirely (e.g. call PropertiesService/game internals directly to read hidden board state or spoof moves).

gas_layered_1.trust.how: Plan addresses client-supplied board tampering and adds identity-based turn/role checks, but never mentions that apiExec/new Function lets any authenticated user execute arbitrary server code (bypassing gameStore entirely) to read hidden fleet/board state directly from PropertiesService; no mitigation like input allowlisting, sandboxing, or restricting apiExec is proposed.

gas_layered_2.trust.how: Plan treats apiExec's new Function(code) RPC channel as trusted transport and only adds server-side authorization inside gameSession.gs (role/turn checks); it never notes that any client can send arbitrary code to apiExec to bypass those checks entirely and read/write PropertiesService state directly, so the eval-based RPC trust boundary itself is neither identified nor mitigated.

gas_layered_3.trust.how: Plan assumes only the client (game.html RPC calls) can trigger moves and gates authority via caller email checks in game-store.gs, but doesn't address that any user can call apiExec directly with arbitrary code via new Function, bypassing game.gs/game-store.gs entirely to read PropertiesService state (revealing hidden fleets/board) or forge moves regardless of role checks.

gas_layeredprops_1.trust.how: Plan focuses on adding persistence/turn-authority via game-store.gs but never mentions that apiExec runs client-submitted code via new Function, letting any page-opener execute arbitrary server code (e.g., bypass playMove and call PropertiesService directly to read/write any game's hidden board state). No sandboxing, RPC allowlisting, or restriction on apiExec is proposed.

gas_layeredprops_2.trust.how: Plan trusts client-claimed identity risk only for gameplay authority (turn/role checks via Session.getActiveUser), but never addresses that apiExec runs arbitrary client-submitted code via new Function, letting any user execute server code as themselves to bypass game-store logic entirely (e.g. call require('common-js/game-store') directly or read PropertiesService state for hidden fleet/board data). No mitigation (e.g. restricting apiExec's allowed functions/module surface, or validating exec payloads) is proposed.

gas_layeredprops_3.trust.how: Plan adds role checks (X/O) and identity via Session.getActiveUser() inside game-store.gs, but never acknowledges that apiExec executes arbitrary client-supplied code via new Function — so any authenticated caller can bypass those role checks entirely (e.g. call PropertiesService/game-store internals directly) and read hidden opponent state. No sandboxing, allowlisting, or code-injection mitigation is proposed.

review_gas_layered_1__focus-trace.judge.correction: Review focuses on join()/play() logic flaws but misses that apiExec executes arbitrary client-submitted code via new Function, letting any user bypass all role/lock checks and directly read/write stored game state.
